title: Cascade Layers with @layer
summary: Set an intentional order for groups of CSS rules.
nestedConcepts: Specificity still applies inside a layer

subtopics.title: Declare a stable layer order
subtopics.explanation: Declare the order of cascade layers near the start of the stylesheet, for example `@layer reset, base, components, utilities;`. Later layers win over earlier layers for normal declarations. A stable order makes it easier for a team to predict which group of styles takes priority.

subtopics.title: Understand layer priority
subtopics.explanation: For normal declarations, a rule in a later layer wins over a rule in an earlier layer before selector specificity is compared. This lets a simple utility class override a more specific component selector when its layer comes later. Important declarations reverse the layer order, so document that exception.

subtopics.title: Specificity still applies inside a layer
subtopics.explanation: Layers decide priority between groups; specificity compares selectors within the same group. For example, `#app .button` can still beat `.button` when both rules are in the same layer. Put rules in intentional layers first, then keep selectors simple to limit specificity conflicts.

subtopics.title: Account for unlayered rules
subtopics.explanation: Normal unlayered author styles outrank normal declarations inside named layers. A third-party stylesheet imported without a layer can therefore override your layered rules unexpectedly. Put dependencies into an explicit layer when possible, and inspect the cascade before increasing selector specificity.

subtopics.title: Organize a stylesheet with layers
subtopics.explanation: Use layers to establish broad styling groups, such as reset, vendor, base, components, and utilities. This creates an explicit priority plan for a growing codebase. Avoid making a new layer for every component; too many groups make the intended cascade harder to see.

foundations.overview: The cascade decides which CSS declaration wins when rules conflict. @layer lets you define a priority order for groups of stylesheets or rules. Layer order is considered before selector specificity, which helps organize resets, components, and utilities.
foundations.mentalModel: It is like deciding which team has priority before comparing individual job titles.
foundations.whyItMatters: It makes large stylesheets easier to reason about than endless specificity escalation.

keyTakeaways: Declare layer order early in the stylesheet.
Later layers have higher priority among normal declarations.
Specificity still matters within a layer.
Unlayered normal styles outrank layered normal styles.
Use layers to define a stable styling architecture.
